idiom_name: struct continuity + dated snapshot array with a hand-written as-of binary search over time_t keys
implementation_notes: C has no classes and no temporal collection, so the roles become plain structs: the continuity is a Contract holding an identity plus an array of { time_t effective; Terms terms; } versions kept sorted by effective, and the as-of lookup is a hand-written upper-bound binary search over that array - the version in force is the last entry whose effective date is not after the query. Effective dates are converted once at the edge with mktime() (or timegm() where the model is calendar-UTC); published entries are never edited, so the update path copies the current Terms, applies the change and inserts the copy at its effective date. When the model really is a database row, a versions table keyed (contract_no, effective_date) with a descending LIMIT 1 query replaces the array.
pitfalls: mktime() interprets struct tm as local time, normalizes out-of-range fields and depends on TZ/DST: pin the timezone or use timegm() for a calendar-UTC model, and note that its (time_t)-1 return is also a legitimate time value.

A Terms struct containing pointers or owned buffers is only shallowly copied, so the old version keeps aliasing the new one's storage; give Terms explicit copy/destroy functions or embed fixed-size values.
The versions array must stay sorted: a retroactive amendment needs a memmove insertion and any blind append must be re-sorted, otherwise the binary search reads garbage without an error.
Concurrent amendments need an explicit lock in the continuity, and a realloc during insertion invalidates every Terms pointer previously handed to callers.
